\section*{Abstract}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Abstract}

We collect 2,921 daily observations of ASML Holding N.V. (2015-01-02 to
2026-08-14) from Yahoo Finance and apply the Box--Jenkins methodology to
determine whether the series can be forecast. Augmented Dickey--Fuller and KPSS
agree that the log price is I(1). An AIC search over sixteen ARIMA orders selects
ARIMA(3,1,3), whose autoregressive and moving-average roots very nearly cancel. A
rolling-origin backtest over 74 origins finds that \textbf{no model beats the
naive forecast by a statistically significant margin at any horizon}, with every
Diebold--Mariano $p$-value against naive above 0.235. We interpret this as a
direct measurement of weak-form market efficiency rather than a modelling
failure.

Two positive results follow. First, the fitted prediction intervals are badly
calibrated, covering 81.5\% of outcomes against a nominal 95\%, which we trace to
the constant-variance assumption that the ARCH-LM test rejects at $p < 0.0001$.
Second, a GARCH(1,1) model shows the \emph{variance} is strongly forecastable,
with persistence 0.9864 and a shock half-life of 50.7 trading days. Extending the
analysis to seven macroeconomic and sector factors reproduces the same conclusion
from a different direction: the semiconductor ETF SOXX correlates 0.8237 with
ASML contemporaneously but only $-0.1210$ at a one-day lead, and a
distributed-lag regression explains 67.95\% of variance with the same-day term
and 1.61\% without it.

\vspace{6pt}
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} Box--Jenkins, ARIMA, exponential smoothing, GARCH,
market efficiency, forecast evaluation, weak-form efficiency.

\section{Introduction and Objective}
\label{sec:intro}

The assignment asks us to collect real stock market data, develop an appropriate
time series model, and forecast future values. We chose ASML Holding N.V., the
Dutch manufacturer that holds an effective monopoly on extreme-ultraviolet
lithography and is therefore a structurally important, highly volatile
semiconductor equity.

Early in the analysis it became clear that the honest deliverable was not a
forecast but a \textbf{verdict on forecastability}. We therefore framed the
project around the question \emph{``How predictable is ASML?''} and answer it
with the tools the course covered. This framing matters: a project that promises
forecasts and delivers noise has failed, whereas a project that asks whether
forecasting is possible and demonstrates rigorously that it is not has succeeded.
The numbers are identical; the scientific claim is not.

\textbf{Scope note.} Sections \ref{sec:data} to \ref{sec:discussion} use only
methods taught in the course: decomposition, ADF and KPSS testing, ACF and PACF
analysis, exponential smoothing, ARIMA, and accuracy measures. Sections
\ref{sec:garch} and \ref{sec:macro} are clearly labelled extension work. GARCH,
Black--Scholes and Granger causality were not covered in the laboratory sessions,
and we present them as such.

\subsection{Data}
\label{sec:introdata}

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Dataset summary.}\label{tab:data}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Property} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
Ticker              & ASML (NASDAQ ADR) \\
Source              & Yahoo Finance via \code{yfinance}, split- and dividend-adjusted \\
Period              & 2015-01-02 to 2026-08-14 (11.6 years) \\
Daily observations  & 2,921 \\
Monthly observations& 140 \\
First close         & 95.94 \\
Last close          & 1,844.08 \\
Total return        & 1,822.0\% \\
CAGR                & 28.98\% \\
Annualised volatility & 38.01\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Daily data is used for stationarity testing, ARIMA and volatility work, where
sample size drives test power. Monthly data (140 points) is used for seasonal
decomposition and exponential smoothing, both of which require a defined seasonal
period that daily trading bars do not possess.

% =====================================================================
\section{Data, Decomposition and Stationarity}
\label{sec:data}

\emph{(Abhinabha Das)}

\subsection{The log transform}

ASML compounded at 28.98\% annually. Growth of that kind is multiplicative, so
its variance grows with its level and violates the constant-variance requirement
of every model that follows. Taking logarithms converts multiplicative growth
into additive growth and stabilises the variance simultaneously. \textbf{All
modelling below is performed on the log price}, with results back-transformed to
price units for reporting.

Daily log returns are strongly non-normal: skewness $-0.3318$ and kurtosis
\textbf{7.8051} against 3.0 for a normal distribution. The fat tails visible in
Figure~\ref{fig:data} recur in the ARIMA residuals (Section~\ref{sec:arima}) and
motivate the Student-$t$ error distribution used for GARCH
(Section~\ref{sec:garch}).

\figw[Log price and daily log returns]{fig_data.png}{0.92}{Price on a log scale
and daily log returns. The log scale turns the compounding into a straight line;
the return panel shows the volatility clustering that Section~\ref{sec:garch}
models directly.}{fig:data}

\subsection{Classical decomposition}

Decomposing the monthly log price into trend, seasonal and remainder components
using \code{seasonal\_decompose} with period 12 gives Hyndman strength measures
as shown in Table~\ref{tab:strength}.

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Decomposition strength measures (0--1).}\label{tab:strength}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Component} & \textbf{Strength} \\
\midrule
Trend    & 0.9905 \\
Seasonal & 0.0980 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[Classical decomposition]{fig_decompose.png}{0.86}{Classical decomposition
of the monthly log price into trend, seasonal and remainder
components.}{fig:decompose}

The series is almost purely trend. A seasonal strength of 0.0980 means the
seasonal panel is fitting noise, not a repeating annual pattern. \textbf{There is
no calendar season in a share price}, and demonstrating that honestly is a result
rather than a disappointment. It sets up a specific prediction for
Section~\ref{sec:smoothing}: the seasonal term in Holt-Winters should earn
nothing. Section~\ref{sec:smoothing} confirms it, with $\gamma$ estimated at
exactly 0.

\figw[Average seasonal effect by month]{fig_seasonal.png}{0.78}{Average seasonal
effect by calendar month. No month departs far enough from zero to be
distinguishable from noise.}{fig:seasonal}

\subsection{Stationarity: ADF and KPSS}
\label{sec:stationarity}

The two tests are constructed with opposite null hypotheses, which is precisely
why they are used together:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{ADF} --- $H_0$: the series has a unit root (non-stationary).
\item \textbf{KPSS} --- $H_0$: the series is stationary.
\end{itemize}

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Stationarity tests on the level and the first difference.}\label{tab:adfkpss}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Series} & \textbf{ADF $p$} & \textbf{KPSS $p$} & \textbf{Verdict} & \textbf{Agree?} \\
\midrule
Log price (level)   & 0.9634    & 0.0100 & Non-stationary & Yes \\
$\Delta$ log price  & $<0.0001$ & 0.1000 & Stationary     & Yes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On the level, ADF cannot reject a unit root and KPSS rejects stationarity; both
point to non-stationarity. After one difference the verdicts invert cleanly.
Because the nulls are opposed, this two-way agreement is considerably stronger
evidence than either test alone. \textbf{ASML log price is I(1), so $d = 1$.}

\subsection{Correlogram}
\label{sec:correlogram}

\figw[ACF and PACF]{fig_acf_pacf.png}{0.92}{ACF and PACF for the log price and
for log returns. The level decays so slowly that lag 40 remains near 1; the
returns collapse into the band immediately.}{fig:acf}

For the log price, \textbf{all 40} autocorrelations exceed the Bartlett band of
$\pm 0.0363$, decaying so slowly that lag 40 remains near 1 --- the textbook
signature of a series with no fixed mean to revert to. For log returns, only
\textbf{9 of 40} exceed the band, and none is large.

A point of honesty is required here. Ljung-Box \cite{ljungbox1978} on returns at
lag 10 gives $p < 0.0001$, so returns are \textbf{not} strictly white noise. With
2,920 observations even an autocorrelation of 0.04 is statistically detectable.
The correct reading is that a trace of linear structure exists and is far too
small to act on --- a distinction that Sections \ref{sec:arima} and
\ref{sec:discussion} quantify precisely.

% =====================================================================
\section{Moving Averages and Exponential Smoothing}
\label{sec:smoothing}

\emph{(K Suraj Das)}

\subsection{Moving averages}

Centred moving averages of 3, 6 and 12 months illustrate the bias--variance
trade-off directly. MA(3) achieves the lowest RMSE because a short window is
permitted to follow the noise, while MA(12) exposes the trend measured at 0.9905
strength in Section~\ref{sec:data}. Neither forecasts anything --- a centred
average cannot reach the ends of the sample.

\subsection{The SES, Holt and Holt-Winters ladder}

All three models were fitted on the same training window and evaluated on the
same twelve-month holdout.

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Fitted smoothing parameters and holdout accuracy.}\label{tab:ets}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ & $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ & $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ & \textbf{Holdout MAPE} \\
\midrule
SES                & 0.9879 & ---    & ---    & 44.68\% \\
Holt               & 0.9371 & 0.0000 & ---    & 39.19\% \\
Holt-Winters (add) & 1.0000 & 0.0000 & 0.0000 & 39.60\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[Holt-Winters fit]{fig_ets.png}{0.86}{Holt-Winters fit on the monthly log
price, with the twelve-month holdout shaded.}{fig:ets}

Three parameter estimates carry the entire story:

\begin{enumerate}
\item $\alpha \approx 1$ for every model. The level is being reset to whatever
just happened, meaning the model is copying the last observation. This is a
random walk wearing a costume.
\item $\beta = 0$ exactly. The trend is estimated as fixed for the whole sample,
which collapses Holt onto a simple drift model.
\item $\gamma = 0$ exactly. Holt-Winters finds no seasonal pattern to learn ---
exactly as Section~\ref{sec:data}'s seasonal strength of 0.0980 predicted.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Comparison against benchmarks}

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Holdout accuracy: models versus benchmarks.}\label{tab:bench}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{MASE} & \textbf{MAPE} & \textbf{Beats naive?} \\
\midrule
SES                & model     & 21.279 & 44.68\% & No  \\
Holt               & model     & 18.625 & 39.19\% & Yes \\
Holt-Winters (add) & model     & 18.653 & 39.60\% & Yes \\
Holt-Winters (mul) & model     & 18.709 & 39.81\% & Yes \\
Naive              & benchmark & 21.248 & 44.61\% & --- \\
Drift              & benchmark & 18.565 & 39.05\% & Yes \\
Seasonal naive     & benchmark & 22.081 & 46.68\% & No  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[Holdout accuracy]{fig_smoothing_errors.png}{0.86}{Holdout accuracy of every
smoother against the three benchmarks.}{fig:smoothing}

\textbf{Drift wins.} Last value plus the average monthly change --- two
parameters, no estimation --- ranks first. Holt collapses onto it once $\beta$ is
estimated at 0, and Holt-Winters adds a seasonal term with $\gamma = 0$ that
changes nothing. The additional machinery buys no accuracy.

\emph{Interpreting MASE correctly.} MASE divides by the \textbf{one-step}
in-sample naive error, so at a twelve-step horizon values well above 1 are
expected and are not evidence of failure \cite{hyndman2021}. What matters is the
ranking and the gap to the same-horizon naive figure of 21.248. Equally, a
twelve-month-ahead MAPE on a stock that tripled says more about the horizon than
about any model, which is why Section~\ref{sec:arima} replaces this single
holdout with a rolling-origin evaluation.

% =====================================================================
\section{ARIMA and Forecast Evaluation}
\label{sec:arima}

\emph{(Akash Kumar)}

\subsection{Order selection}

With $d = 1$ fixed by Section~\ref{sec:stationarity}, we searched all sixteen
combinations of $p, q \in \{0,1,2,3\}$ by AIC. \code{pmdarima}'s
\code{auto\_arima} is unavailable under NumPy 2, so the grid is explicit --- which
is in any case more defensible, since every candidate is visible.

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{AIC ranking of the candidate ARIMA orders (abridged).}\label{tab:aic}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Order} & \textbf{AIC} & \textbf{$\Delta$AIC} \\
\midrule
(3,1,3)                  & $-13{,}539.73$ & 0.00  \\
(1,1,3)                  & $-13{,}520.20$ & 19.53 \\
(0,1,3)                  & $-13{,}515.40$ & 24.33 \\
(1,1,0)                  & $-13{,}515.37$ & 24.36 \\
\multicolumn{3}{c}{\dots} \\
(0,1,0) --- random walk  & $-13{,}502.80$ & 36.93 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[AIC across candidate orders]{fig_arima_grid.png}{0.86}{AIC across all
sixteen candidate orders. The pure random walk sits last.}{fig:grid}

The pure random walk ranks \textbf{sixteenth of sixteen}, 36.93 AIC units behind.
AIC therefore does detect genuine structure in the differenced series; this is
not a case of the criterion being unable to choose.

\subsection{Estimates, and why they mislead}
\label{sec:roots}

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{ARIMA(3,1,3) coefficient estimates.}\label{tab:coef}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Coefficient} & \textbf{Estimate} \\
\midrule
ar.L1 & $-0.7897$ \\
ar.L2 & 0.8681 \\
ar.L3 & 0.9119 \\
ma.L1 & 0.7384 \\
ma.L2 & $-0.8740$ \\
ma.L3 & $-0.8520$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All six coefficients are significant at 5\%, and estimates of this size look like
powerful evidence of structure. They are not. What matters is not the
coefficients but the roots of the two polynomials they define.

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Root moduli of the fitted AR and MA polynomials.}\label{tab:roots}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
\toprule
& \textbf{Root moduli} \\
\midrule
AR(3) & 1.0026,\; 1.0458,\; 1.0458 \\
MA(3) & 1.0035,\; 1.0815,\; 1.0815 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Every root lies outside the unit circle, so the model is stationary and
invertible --- but only barely, and that is the point. The smallest AR root and
the smallest MA root are \textbf{1.0026 and 1.0035}: they sit almost exactly on
top of one another, and both sit almost exactly \emph{on} the unit circle. A root
at 1 on the AR side is a unit root; a matching root at 1 on the MA side cancels
it. The two polynomials therefore share a \textbf{near-common factor very close
to $(1 - L)$} --- and a factor that appears on both sides of the equation does no
forecasting work at all. Six large, individually significant coefficients are
spending themselves on a matched pair that annihilates, and what survives is a
process barely distinguishable from the random walk we already differenced away.

This is the most important caveat in the report. \textbf{A model can carry large,
individually significant coefficients and still describe a process barely
distinguishable from a random walk.} Reading the coefficient table alone would
give exactly the opposite impression; reading the roots gives it away
immediately, and only an out-of-sample test can settle it.

\figw[Thirty-day forecast]{fig_forecast.png}{0.86}{Thirty-day forecast with 80\%
and 95\% prediction intervals. The path is nearly flat, as a near-random walk
implies; the honest content of the forecast is its width.}{fig:forecast}

\subsection{Residual diagnostics, and a trap worth documenting}
\label{sec:burnin}

\code{statsmodels} \cite{statsmodels2010} initialises its state-space filter from
a diffuse prior, so the first residual is not a model error but the filter
finding its footing. On this series that residual is \textbf{4.5638} against a
residual standard deviation of \textbf{0.0237} --- a \textbf{192.2-sigma}
observation.

Left in, it dominates every sum of squares that follows and Ljung-Box reports
$p = 0.99999$: apparently flawless white noise. After trimming, the same test
reports $p = 0.0961$ --- an order of magnitude from a rejection rather than a
hair's breadth from certainty. \textbf{The entire appearance of a perfect fit
rested on a single observation}, and nothing in the output looks wrong when it
happens. Every diagnostic in this project routes through one shared trimming
helper for that reason.

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Residual diagnostics with the burn-in observation excluded.}\label{tab:resid}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcl@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Test} & \textbf{$p$-value} & \textbf{Conclusion} \\
\midrule
Ljung-Box (10)              & 0.0961    & No autocorrelation left at 5\% \\
Jarque-Bera                 & $<0.0001$ & Not normal (kurtosis 7.2615) \\
ARCH-LM (10)                & $<0.0001$ & Variance is not constant \\
Ljung-Box on squared residuals & $<0.0001$ & Variance has memory \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[Residual diagnostics]{fig_arima_resid.png}{0.92}{Residual series, ACF and
normal Q--Q plot for the fitted ARIMA(3,1,3).}{fig:resid}

The mean model is clean: with burn-in excluded the residuals pass the white-noise
test at 5\%, which is what a correctly specified ARIMA should deliver. The
remaining three results are not defects in it but \textbf{findings} about the
data. Fat tails \cite{jarquebera1980} and clustered variance \cite{engle1982} are
what daily equity returns genuinely look like, and the ARCH result is the direct
motivation for Section~\ref{sec:garch}. Note what this combination means: the
model has extracted all the \emph{linear} structure there was to extract, and the
backtest below still cannot beat a naive forecast with it.

\subsection{Rolling-origin backtest}
\label{sec:backtest}

A single holdout is one draw. We refit at \textbf{74} successive origins with an
expanding window and scored every model at horizons of 1, 3 and 6 months.

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{MASE by forecast horizon across 74 rolling origins.}\label{tab:mase}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{$h=1$} & \textbf{$h=3$} & \textbf{$h=6$} \\
\midrule
ARIMA(3,1,3) & 7.179 & 13.558 & 24.483 \\
Holt         & 7.114 & 13.498 & 25.612 \\
Naive        & 7.151 & 13.634 & 24.556 \\
Drift        & 7.020 & 13.211 & 23.273 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Diebold--Mariano $p$-values against naive, Newey--West corrected for the
overlap that multi-step forecasts create.}\label{tab:dm}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{$h=1$} & \textbf{$h=3$} & \textbf{$h=6$} \\
\midrule
ARIMA & 0.634 & 0.307 & 0.235 \\
Holt  & 0.880 & 0.888 & 0.722 \\
Drift & 0.507 & 0.582 & 0.603 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[MASE by horizon]{fig_backtest.png}{0.86}{MASE by forecast horizon. The
models and the benchmarks are indistinguishable within sampling
error.}{fig:backtest}

\textbf{Not one $p$-value falls below 0.05.} Drift ranks first at every horizon,
but a ranking without a significant margin is not a win --- and reporting it as
one would be the single easiest error to make in this project. The
Diebold--Mariano test \cite{dieboldmariano1995} exists precisely to prevent it.

\subsection{Prediction interval coverage}
\label{sec:coverage}

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Empirical coverage of the nominal 95\% prediction
intervals.}\label{tab:coverage}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Horizon} & \textbf{Empirical coverage} & \textbf{Nominal} \\
\midrule
$h = 1$ & 82.4\% & 95\% \\
$h = 3$ & 82.4\% & 95\% \\
$h = 6$ & 79.7\% & 95\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Mean coverage is \textbf{81.5\%} against a nominal 95\%. The intervals are
\textbf{too narrow} --- the model systematically understates risk. The cause is
identified in Section~\ref{sec:burnin}: ARIMA assumes one constant error variance
while ARCH-LM rejects that assumption outright. Averaging volatility across calm
and turbulent regimes understates risk in exactly the periods where it matters
most.

We report this deliberately. It is the honest limitation of the model we actually
fitted, and it is the gap Section~\ref{sec:garch} exists to close.

% =====================================================================
\section{Discussion: Interpreting a Null Result}
\label{sec:discussion}

Four independent lines of evidence, drawn from four different laboratory
sessions, converge:

\begin{enumerate}
\item ADF and KPSS \cite{kpss1992} agree the log price is I(1)
      (Section~\ref{sec:stationarity}).
\item The ACF of returns collapses immediately, with the largest autocorrelation
      far below any tradeable size (Section~\ref{sec:correlogram}).
\item The selected ARIMA's AR and MA roots nearly cancel, describing a
      near-random walk (Section~\ref{sec:roots}).
\item No model beats naive out of sample at any horizon, with
      $\mathrm{DM}\ p \geq 0.235$ (Section~\ref{sec:backtest}).
\end{enumerate}

Convergent evidence of this kind is a stronger empirical argument than any single
model with a flattering error metric. It is also a textbook result: this is the
empirical content of \textbf{weak-form market efficiency} \cite{fama1970}. If past
prices contained exploitable information, trading activity would already have
removed it. Our inability to beat a naive forecast is a confirmation of
established theory measured on data we collected ourselves, not a failure of
method.

The failure mode we deliberately avoided was tuning horizons, orders and windows
until something appeared to win. Given enough specifications, one will win by
chance; the Diebold--Mariano test is what distinguishes that from a real effect.

% =====================================================================
\section{Extension: Volatility and Option Pricing}
\label{sec:garch}

\emph{(Ritesh K R)} --- \textbf{beyond the course syllabus}

\subsection{GARCH(1,1)}

Section~\ref{sec:arima} left two loose ends pointing the same way: ARCH-LM
rejected constant variance, and the prediction intervals covered 81.5\% instead
of 95\%. GARCH(1,1) \cite{bollerslev1986} addresses both by letting today's
variance depend on yesterday's shock and yesterday's variance, with Student-$t$
errors to accommodate kurtosis of 7.8051.

\begin{equation}
\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2
\end{equation}

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Fitted GARCH(1,1) parameters.}\label{tab:garch}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Estimate} \\
\midrule
$\alpha$ (shock)               & 0.0752 \\
$\beta$ (persistence)          & 0.9113 \\
$\alpha + \beta$               & 0.9864 \\
Half-life                      & 50.7 trading days \\
Current annualised volatility  & 45.3\% \\
Long-run annualised volatility & 42.7\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[GARCH conditional volatility]{fig_garch_vol.png}{0.86}{GARCH(1,1)
conditional volatility. Shocks decay slowly, which is what a persistence of
0.9864 means in practice.}{fig:garch}

Persistence of 0.9864 means a volatility shock is still half-present roughly 50
trading days later. Ljung-Box on the squared standardised residuals returns
$p = 0.2012$, so the model has fully absorbed the ARCH effect that ARIMA left
behind.

\textbf{This is the project's central contrast: the direction of ASML is
unforecastable, but the magnitude of its moves is strongly forecastable.}

\subsection{Black--Scholes against a live market}

We priced 61 near-the-money calls expiring 2026-09-18 using the GARCH volatility
of 45.3\% and a risk-free rate of 3.697\% taken from the 13-week Treasury bill
\cite{blackscholes1973}.

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Model price against the live option chain at the money.}\label{tab:bs}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Quantity} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
Spot                     & 1,844.08 \\
ATM strike               & 1,840.00 \\
Market mid               & 102.85 \\
Black--Scholes price     & 105.09 \\
Difference               & $+2.2\%$ \\
Mean implied volatility  & 49.2\% \\
GARCH volatility         & 45.3\% \\
Gap                      & $+3.9$ points \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[Model versus market, and the smile]{fig_options.png}{0.92}{Model versus
market prices across strikes, and the implied volatility smile.}{fig:options}

The market prices 3.9 volatility points above what history alone justifies --- the
standard interpretation being a variance risk premium plus event risk inside the
expiry. More revealing is the \textbf{smile}: Black--Scholes assumes a single
volatility for every strike, yet implied volatility curves visibly across
moneyness. Both departures trace to the same wrong assumption --- constant
Gaussian volatility --- that Section~\ref{sec:arima}'s ARCH test and residual
kurtosis of 7.2615 had already rejected.

\section{Extension: Macro-Factor Lag Analysis}
\label{sec:macro}

\emph{(Aditya Mehta)} --- \textbf{beyond the course syllabus}

If ASML cannot predict itself, can anything else? We tested seven factors over
2,915 common trading days.

\subsection{Cross-correlation}

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Contemporaneous correlation against the best one-day
lead.}\label{tab:ccf}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Factor} & \textbf{Same day (lag 0)} & \textbf{Best lead (lag $+1$)} & \textbf{Ratio} \\
\midrule
SOXX (semiconductor ETF)  & 0.8237    & $-0.1210$ & 0.15 \\
TSM (customer)            & 0.6780    & $-0.0836$ & 0.12 \\
\code{\^{}GSPC} (S\&P 500) & 0.6728    & $-0.1466$ & 0.22 \\
NVDA                      & 0.6304    & $-0.0724$ & 0.11 \\
\code{\^{}VIX}            & $-0.5253$ & 0.0690    & 0.13 \\
\code{\^{}TNX} (10Y yield)& 0.0801    & $-0.0822$ & 1.03 \\
EURUSD=X                  & 0.0068    & $-0.0445$ & 6.54 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[Cross-correlation across leads and lags]{fig_macro_ccf.png}{0.92}{Cross-correlation
across leads and lags. Every factor shows a tall spike at lag 0 and near-flat
ground on either side.}{fig:ccf}

Every factor shows the same shape: a tall spike at lag 0 and near-flat ground on
either side. \textbf{Not one factor carries a usable lead.} Note also that the
lag-1 correlations are \emph{negative} --- the opposite sign to the same-day
relationship. That is the signature of short-horizon reversal and bid-ask bounce,
not of a predictive link; a factor genuinely leading ASML would carry the same
sign it has at lag 0.

\subsection{Distributed-lag regression}
\label{sec:dlag}

Regressing ASML returns on SOXX and five of its lags gives the contrast in
Table~\ref{tab:dlag}.

\begin{table}[H]\centering
\caption{Explanatory power with and without the same-day term.}\label{tab:dlag}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Specification} & \textbf{$R^2$} \\
\midrule
Including the same-day term              & 0.6795 \\
Lags only (what a forecaster could use)  & 0.0161 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\figw[Distributed lag coefficients]{fig_macro_dlag.png}{0.80}{Distributed lag
coefficients on SOXX. The lag-0 term dwarfs every lagged one.}{fig:dlag}

The lag-0 coefficient is 0.9381 and dwarfs every lagged term. \textbf{Removing
the one variable a forecaster cannot know in advance destroys 97.6\% of the
explanatory power.} High correlation and zero predictability coexist comfortably,
and that is the most useful thing this section has to say.

\subsection{Granger causality}

Testing lags 1 to 5 per factor with a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of
$\alpha = 0.01$ \cite{granger1969}:

\textbf{Four factors are Granger-significant: SOXX, TSM, \code{\^{}GSPC} and
\code{\^{}TNX}.}

We report this plainly rather than suppressing it, because it appears to cut
against the section's conclusion. It does not, for two reasons. First,
significance and usefulness are different questions: across 2,915 observations a
test will detect an effect explaining well under 1\% of variance, which is exactly
what Section~\ref{sec:dlag} measures directly. Second, Section~\ref{sec:arima}
already demonstrated what becomes of small in-sample effects when taken out of
sample. The honest summary is that these factors carry a \textbf{statistically
real but economically negligible} lead.

Granger causality is also a claim about forecast improvement, not about cause.
The test cannot distinguish whether a factor drives ASML, responds to it, or
shares a common driver with it --- and for a chip-equipment maker and a
semiconductor index, the third is by far the most plausible.

% =====================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Single asset, single regime.} Conclusions are specific to ASML over
2015--2026, a period dominated by one extraordinary bull run.
\item \textbf{Linear models only.} ARIMA and exponential smoothing capture linear
dependence. A non-linear or regime-switching relationship would be invisible to
every test used here.
\item \textbf{SARIMA was not fitted.} The course covered it only as a next step,
and Section~\ref{sec:data} measured seasonal strength at 0.0980, so a seasonal
ARIMA was not justified. It remains the natural extension.
\item \textbf{Daily closes ignore microstructure.} Bid-ask bounce plausibly
explains the negative lag-1 correlations in Section~\ref{sec:macro}; intraday
data would be needed to confirm this.
\item \textbf{Live option chain.} Section~\ref{sec:garch} reflects quotes at one
moment; liquidity varies by strike and stale quotes can distort implied
volatilities in the wings.
\item \textbf{No transaction costs.} Even had a model beaten naive, costs were
not modelled, so no claim about tradeable profit could follow.
\end{enumerate}

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Applying the Box--Jenkins methodology \cite{boxjenkins1970} to 2,921 daily
observations of ASML, we find the log price is I(1); that an AIC-selected
ARIMA(3,1,3) carries six significant coefficients whose AR and MA roots nearly
cancel; and that across 74 rolling origins \textbf{no model beats the naive
forecast by a statistically significant margin at any horizon}. Four independent
lines of evidence converge on the same conclusion, which we identify as weak-form
market efficiency rather than a modelling failure.

Two findings extend beyond that null result. The fitted prediction intervals are
materially miscalibrated at 81.5\% empirical coverage against 95\% nominal, and
the cause is the constant-variance assumption that ARCH-LM rejects. Modelling the
variance directly with GARCH(1,1) yields persistence of 0.9864 and a 50.7-day
shock half-life, fully absorbing the ARCH effect. The practical summary is the one
we would defend in a viva: \textbf{we cannot say where ASML is going, but we can
say --- with a well-specified model --- how rough the journey will be.}

\section*{Appendix: Reproducibility}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix: Reproducibility}

Every figure and every number in this report is generated by
\code{docs/figures/make\_figures.py}, which imports the same backend modules that
serve the project dashboard. There is one implementation, so a figure in this
report cannot disagree with the application.

\begin{quote}
\code{pip install -r backend/requirements.txt}\\
\code{python docs/figures/make\_figures.py}\quad --- figures and \code{facts.json}\\
\code{pytest backend/test\_backend.py}\quad --- 55 assertions, including the burn-in guard\\
\code{python -m uvicorn main:app --port 8000}\quad --- from \code{backend/}\\
\code{npm run dev}\quad --- dashboard at port 5173
\end{quote}

Because the data is fetched live, re-running after a market move will shift the
final digits. The structural conclusions --- I(1), near-cancelling roots, no
significant edge over naive, high GARCH persistence --- are stable across
refreshes. \code{backend/test\_backend.py} asserts them, so if a future refresh
ever overturns the headline result, the test suite fails and this report needs
rewriting rather than the test.
